activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Arthur had been to Emelia's house a dozen times, but he had never been past the kitchen until Saturday, when her mother asked if he wanted to help with the surprise. Emelia's grandmother was turning eighty, and the plan was a board of family photographs to hang above the cake table. Emelia spread the pictures across the living room carpet like a giant game of memory, and Arthur's job was to sort them into two piles, nice ones and extra nice ones.

He worked through them one by one. There was Emelia at age six gap-toothed on a tropical beach, there was her parents' wedding, there was a cousin graduation. Then he found a wide photo of a whole family standing in rows, everyone dressed in plain white shirts and white headbands. It looked formal and calm, like the kind of picture taken at a wedding. He set it in the extra nice pile, right beside a photo of Emelia's aunt in a lacy white gown cutting a cake.

When Emelia came back with lemonade, she stood over the piles with her hands on her hips. "Good," she said, tapping the wedding picture. Then her finger stopped on the family in white. "Why did you put this one there?"

"It's a wedding," Arthur said. "Everybody's in white, like your aunt."

Emelia picked it up and studied it the way Ms. De Vries studied a suspicious book report. "This is my great-grandmother's funeral," she said finally. "Everybody's wearing white. In traditional Chinese culture, white is worn for mourning at funerals."

Arthur looked at the two photos side by side, one family in white for a funeral, one bride in white for a wedding, and felt his whole sorting system wobble. "So white can mean two opposite things?"

"Apparently." Emelia set the funeral photo gently in a third pile she made on the arm of the couch. "I didn't know that either until I asked my mom last year. I used to think Western brides were copying us, but it's just different."

Arthur wanted to make sure he had it right before they glued anything down. At the party a week later, he watched for himself. Emelia's grandmother, dressed in deep red, laughed at the photo board, and when she reached the funeral picture she touched the edge of the frame and said something quiet in Cantonese to Emelia's mother. Later, at the cake table, the grandmother pointed at Arthur and asked Emelia a question. Emelia translated: she wants to know why you keep staring at everybody's clothes.

"She's checking something," Emelia said, grinning.

Arthur admitted it. He had counted, and in every photo from the wedding side the bride wore white, and in every photo from the funeral side the whole family wore white, and now he was watching the guests to see if anyone would show up to the party in white by accident. The grandmother listened, then shook her head at him with warm, amused eyes.

"Wear red," she said in English, and patted the sleeve of her own crimson blouse.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
Clara had thirty-two dollars in her pocket and one goal: buy a ticket to the Silver Comets concert at the mall kiosk before anyone else did. The tickets were twenty dollars, which was the whole point. Her friend Raiden had texted her that morning: "Tickets go on sale at NOON. The line starts at the pretzel stand. Bring snacks. This is not leisure, this is war."

By eleven-thirty, the line curved past the pretzel stand, around the fountain, and halfway to the shoe store. Clara counted heads as she walked. She got to one hundred and forty and gave up, because the line kept going. Behind the kiosk counter, Mr. Yamamoto was stacking a small box on top of the register. Clara stood on her toes. The box was shallow. She did the math in her head and felt something go brittle in her chest, like a pretzel snapped in half. One hundred forty people, probably more, and maybe fifty tickets. Maybe fewer. She couldn't see the exact number, but she could see the shape of the problem, and the shape was bad.

At noon the line surged. Twenty minutes later Mr. Yamamoto flipped the sign to SOLD OUT, and a groan rolled down the corridor like a wave. A girl near the front held her ticket over her head and cheered, which did not help. Clara was still a hundred people back. She stomped toward the food court, where Raiden sat with an empty plate and a grim expression. "I had two thoughts on the walk over," he said. "Thought one: pretzels without cheese are a crime. Thought two: they priced those tickets too low. At twenty dollars, everybody in this mall wanted one, and there weren't enough for everybody."

Clara slid into the seat across from him. "My sister would call that a shortage," she said. "When a price is kept below the, uh, the right price, more people want the thing than there are things for sale." She'd overheard the phrase once and now it clicked into place like a puzzle piece. "So here's my test. If that's true, the tickets that exist should be worth more than twenty dollars now. Watch what happens."

They watched. Near the escalator, the girl who had cheered was surrounded by three boys, cash in hand. "Sixty," one said. "Eighty," said another. The girl grinned and held up a finger, making them wait. Clara leaned toward Raiden and whispered, "Tickets left the store in twenty minutes. Hundreds of fans got nothing. And the price just went up on its own, like it knew." Raiden pulled out his phone and started typing. "I'm messaging my cousin. She has a birthday next week and zero patience." He turned the screen so Clara could read it: "Dear Cousin, I have survived the Ticket War of the Mall. I fought bravely. I lost. Send money. Love, Raiden." The girl by the escalator pocketed her eighty dollars, and the boys chased the next ticket down the corridor.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Joshua's mom had left for the weekend with one instruction taped to the washer: "Dark clothes together, cold water, don't shrink my sweater." That meant the laundry was his, all of it, and Wesley had come over mostly to watch and partly because he wanted his lucky shirt washed before Monday's tryouts. "It's my tryout shirt," Wesley said, holding it out like evidence. "Kevin's mom does his, but my mom says I'm old enough now."

They sorted piles on the kitchen floor, argued about whether gray counted as dark, and ran two loads. When everything came out damp and wrinkled, Joshua remembered the iron in the hall closet. His dad used it for work shirts, and it had a dial with names like cotton and wool and a little chart of symbols on the handle. Joshua turned it to cotton, the hottest-sounding setting, because cotton seemed like it should mean business.

The trouble was Wesley's shirt. It was some shiny game-day material, and when Joshua pressed the iron onto the sleeve, a patch of it went dull and flat, like frost on a window. "What did you do?" Wesley grabbed the shirt and stared at the shiny spot. "This is my tryout shirt." Joshua's first motive for hiding the iron behind his back was simple: Wesley looked ready to tackle him. But then he turned the iron over and saw the symbol on the shirt's tag, a little iron outline with two dots inside it, and below the handle's chart, tiny words matched dots to settings. One dot meant low, about 110 degrees Celsius. Two dots meant medium, about 150. Three dots meant high, about 200.

"Wait," Joshua said. "Your shirt has two dots. That's medium, 150 degrees. I had it on cotton, which is the high setting, 200." He tested the idea right there, turning the dial down to the two-dot level and pressing a corner of his own sock. Nothing went shiny. The sock came out smooth and unharmed, which was more than he could say for Wesley's sleeve.

"We could tell people it's a lightning bolt," Wesley said, holding the sleeve up to the light. "Like it's intentional. Influential athletes have custom gear all the time." Joshua did his best to reassure him. "It's small. Nobody at tryouts will be close enough to see it, and if they are, they'll think you iron your own clothes, which is basically true now."

Wesley put the shirt on right there, damp and all, and stood in front of the hallway mirror flexing his arm so the patch caught the light. "Lightning bolt," he said again, and this time he almost sounded convinced. Joshua folded the last towel, set it on the stack, and turned the iron off with two fingers.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
story:
Everly spread her flashcards across the library table, careful not to let them slide into the study carrel next to hers. Mr. Pham had assigned a spoken presentation for Friday: describe your family and pets in Mandarin, using full sentences. She could already say that her mother liked tea and that her cat, Biscuit, was lazy and gray. The trouble was her brother, Henry.

At the next table, Jamie was mouthing vocabulary words with a pencil tucked behind one ear. Everly leaned over. "What word are you using for your sister?" she asked.

"Mèimei. She's younger than me, so it's mèimei." Jamie set the pencil down. "Why, what's wrong?"

"My flashcard just says 'brother.' But there are two words, right? One for older and one for younger."

Jamie flipped to the back of the textbook, where a family chart filled a whole page. "Gēge means older brother," Jamie said, tapping the page. "And dìdi means younger brother. It's right here."

Everly copied both words onto fresh cards, then stopped. Henry was her twin. They shared a birthday, a bedroom, and an unreasonable number of arguments about whose turn it was to feed Biscuit. Ten minutes, though. Her mother told the story every year: Everly at 7:42, Henry at 7:52. Ten minutes older. That was all the difference there was.

She tried to say her sentence out loud, quietly, and it came out wrong twice before it came out right. "Wǒ yǒu yí gè dìdi," she whispered. It felt strange, calling her twin a younger brother, but the rule did not care how strange it felt. Ten minutes was still older, which made him still younger, which made him dìdi.

She remembered a night last winter when the two of them sat on the kitchen floor building a card tower, and Henry insisted that being born second made him the baby of the family forever. Everly had argued back then that twins were exactly equal. Now she had vocabulary proving otherwise, and she could not wait to tell him.

For Friday's presentation, Mr. Pham wanted them to articulate each sentence clearly, not just mumble sounds. Everly practiced until the words felt smooth. Describing her family in full sentences was more work than listing names, but it was feasible if she practiced a little every day, and her flashcards were holding up better than the flimsy set she had made for Spanish, which had fallen apart within a week. She had a whole new constitution for these, index cards with packing tape along the edges.

On Friday morning, before class, she found Henry at his locker. "Guess what," she said. "In Mandarin, I have to call you dìdi. You're my younger brother."

"By ten minutes," Henry said, slamming the locker door.

"Ten minutes is ten minutes," said Everly, and she grinned all the way down the hall.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Facing a person with hearing loss and speaking clearly helps them understand more than shouting does.
story:
Grandpa Ray arrived on Sunday with one duffel bag and a joke about how the airline had lost his hearing, not his luggage. Alicia laughed, but by Tuesday she was tired of repeating herself. She would call from the kitchen, "Do you want lemonade?" and he would answer "Tuesday already?" She tried shouting louder and louder, until her throat hurt and he still guessed wrong. That night she wrote in her notebook: Grandpa problem. Shouting does not work. Why?

On Wednesday, Libby came over and they set up a experiment in the backyard. Alicia stood by the fence and asked Grandpa a question with her back turned. He got it wrong. Then she tried again, shouting across the whole yard. Wrong again, and he looked annoyed, too. Libby tilted her head. "When my mom can't hear me, she always says to come stand in front of her." Alicia wasn't sure that made sense, since shouting was louder than talking. But that was the point of testing ideas. She walked right up to Grandpa's chair, crouched so they were face to face, and asked slowly and clearly, "Do you want lemonade?" Grandpa smiled before she even finished. "I'd love some. And a cookie, if you're offering."

Alicia felt like a scientist who had just diagnosed the real trouble. It wasn't volume at all. Being face to face and speaking clearly helped him understand more than shouting did. She tested it for two more days, on purpose. She tested it in the noisy kitchen with the blender going, and in the quiet backyard. She tested short sentences and long ones. The pattern held every time, even when Bo stopped by and forgot, yelling "Mr. Ray, nice garden!" from the patio door. Grandpa frowned at his crossword. Bo walked over, repeated it, and got a grin and a thumbs up.

By Friday, Alicia had trained the whole backyard. When Bo set up the badminton net too close to Grandpa's chair, he jogged over to say so instead of hollering. When Libby found a toad behind the shed, she brought it over to show him rather than announcing it from across the grass. Grandpa held the toad and told a long, eloquent story about catching them as a boy in Ohio, waving one hand in circles, and nobody had to ask him to repeat a single part.

On the last evening, Grandpa settled into his chair with a blanket while Alicia set the badminton rackets by the back door. She crouched down in front of him, like she always did now. "One more game before it gets dark?" Grandpa was already standing. "Race you to the net," he said.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A company can cut or skip the dividends it pays stockholders, but missing a promised interest payment on its bonds counts as a default.
story:
Emily sat on the hard bench near the loan desk while her mother filled out a form at the counter. On her lap sat two papers: her own savings statement, and a page her brother had printed from his account. She was supposed to give a short talk in Mr. Mwangi's class on Friday about which was riskier, a stock or a bond, and so far all she knew was that both could come from the same company.

She had ten shares of Brightlane Media, a company she'd picked because she liked its shows. Her brother had a Brightlane bond. Last quarter, her statement showed a dividend, small but real. This quarter it showed nothing at all.

"Kaden," she whispered to her friend, who had tagged along to get a roll of quarters for the arcade, "look at this. My dividend's gone. Just gone."

Kaden leaned over. "Did the company die?"

"I don't think so. My brother's statement came yesterday and his Brightlane bond still paid him. Same company, same month. His money showed up and mine didn't." She frowned at the page. "So the bond is safer? But everyone says stocks are the ones that grow."

The bank's front door opened and Julius hurried in out of the rain, shaking water off his jacket. He spotted them and came over. "Mr. Mwangi still want the risk talk?" he asked. "I'm doing weather. Easy. Voltage from lightning, clouds, done."

"Show-off," Emily said, but she was barely listening. She pulled her brother's page out of her folder and laid the two statements side by side on the bench. Both had the same company name. Hers had a blank where the dividend should be. His had a payment, right there in the interest column. "He gets paid because it's promised," she said slowly. "Mine can just stop."

"That seems backwards," Kaden said. "Your money's the one taking the risk, but his is the one that's safe?"

Emily thought about the lightning talk Julius was planning. Lightning you could see, at least. This was invisible, a rule hiding inside the paper. She had an idea for how to test it. "Watch. If I'm right, the word for it is somewhere in this folder." She dug through the papers her brother had given her until she found a booklet about bonds, and flipped through it until she reached the section on what could go wrong.

"There." She pointed at a line and read it under her breath. Then she looked up, grinning. "It's called a default. If the company misses a promised interest payment on its bond, that's a default. But with a stock, cutting or skipping the dividend doesn't count as one. They're allowed to do that to me." She stacked the pages. "I'm the pessimistic investor here, apparently. I need a snack to consume before I write any more of this."

Her mother waved from the counter, done with her form. Emily scooped up the folder and held it up so Kaden and Julius could see. "The bond's the safer one. Same company, and my dividend vanished while his payment showed up. That's my whole talk, right there."

"Friday's going to be rough on Brightlane," Julius said, and held the door for all of them.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Henry climbed out of the pool on Tuesday feeling great. His arms were tired, sure, but he'd made the community swim team, and first practice had gone better than he expected. Fifty push-ups on the deck, a hundred flutter kicks holding the wall, and then laps until Mr. Thompson blew his whistle.

"You'll want to take the stairs slowly tomorrow," said Imane, wringing out her ponytail beside him. "Trust me."

Tomorrow? Henry laughed. He felt fine now. At home he did his chores, ate two sandwiches, and slept like a rock.

Thursday morning he woke up and could barely sit up. His shoulders screamed when he lifted his arms to brush his teeth, and his thighs burned so much that he gripped the railing and lowered himself down the stairs sideways, one step at a time, like his grandfather. His mom asked if he'd hurt himself. He hadn't, he was sure of it, but he couldn't explain why the pain had shown up two full days after practice instead of right after it. That seemed backward. Injuries hurt immediately, didn't they? He thought about it through math class, doodling a little timeline in his notebook: practice Tuesday, fine Tuesday, wrecked Thursday.

At the pool that afternoon he found Imane already in the water, swimming slow, careful laps. She had her own goal this season: she wanted the coach to move her up a lane, and she was terrified that a bad week would exclude her from the relay lineup. When Henry told her he was thinking of quitting because his body clearly couldn't handle this, she stopped mid-stroke. "It happens to everyone after the first hard week," she said. "My brother calls it delayed onset muscle soreness. It peaks somewhere between twenty-four and seventy-two hours later, not right away." Henry stared at her. Seventy-two hours. Thursday was exactly two days after Tuesday. That matched his timeline doodle perfectly. His body wasn't broken; it was just running on a delay.

So he tested it. Instead of quitting, he swam an easy practice, half speed, letting his sore muscles move through the water. By Saturday the ache had faded to a dull hum, and by Monday he felt almost normal. Mr. Thompson posted the relay roster on the locker room door, and Imane scanned it with her towel clutched in both fists. Her name was in the second heat. She spun around and grabbed Henry's shoulder. "Second lane up! I made it!"

"Next season," Henry said, "remind me about the two-day thing before I panic." He pulled his cap on and walked to the blocks, taking the stairs two at a time.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
Jessica sat on the floor of her nearly empty bedroom, taping the last box shut, while her mom directed the movers in the hall. In three days she would be in apartment 6B in a town four hours away, and her best friends Charlize and Mario would still be here.

"Every time somebody moves, they say they'll stay in touch, and then they don't," Jessica said. "My cousin moved two years ago and she never talks to her old friends anymore. I keep trying to figure out why some friendships fade and some don't."

Mario spun a roll of tape on his finger. "Maybe it's random. Some people just drift."

"That contradicts what I've seen, though," Jessica said. "Remember when Charlize switched schools in fifth grade? She still sees her old friend all the time, and I bet I know why. I'm going to test it." She pulled out her notebook. The night before Charlize's move back then, the two of them had written something on a calendar at Charlize's kitchen table, and they had kept it going for three whole years.

"Charlize!" Jessica shouted down the hall. "What did you and Rosa do before she moved?"

Charlize appeared in the doorway, holding two slices of pizza. "We picked Sunday afternoons for video calls. Every single Sunday, whether we felt like it or not. Sometimes it was only ten minutes."

Jessica wrote it down. "That's the factor, isn't it? It's not luck. My cousin never scheduled anything, she just said 'text me anytime,' and nobody did. But you two had a regular time, so it never dropped." She tapped the notebook. "Friendships fade when people who move apart just wait around. The ones that stay close are the ones who keep in touch on a schedule, calls or messages or visits."

"So set one before the truck leaves," Mario said. "That's your test."

Jessica grabbed her phone and opened the calendar, then hesitated. Making a promise felt impulsive, and she hated breaking promises. "Wednesday at seven?" she said. "Right after dinner, before homework."

"Wednesday at seven," Charlize said, and Mario added himself to the call from his own phone so all three names sat in a row on the screen.

Her mom called from the front door that the truck was loaded. Jessica hugged them both fast and hard, then ran down the stairs, phone buzzing in her pocket with the calendar reminder already set. Wednesday, 7:00 p.m., she read, as the truck pulled away.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing.
story:
Sofia had written the same sentence seven times, and it still looked wrong. Her notebook lay open beside a mug of hot chocolate at the corner table of the cafe, where the window fogged with vapor from the kitchen until she wiped a small circle to see the street through it.

"You look like you're trying to conceal a crime," said Maxwell, sliding into the seat across from her with a muffin the size of his fist.

"It's my story for Ms. Moretti," Sofia said. "Two characters argue in it, and every time I write what they say, the punctuation turns into an intricate mess." She turned the notebook so he could see the draft. The line read: "I never took your compass," Mom said. "and you can't prove it."

Maxwell chewed his muffin and squinted at the page. "The second part starts with a capital A, right? So that's fine."

"That's what I thought." Sofia tapped her pencil against the mug. "But listen to it in your head. 'I never took your comma pause and you can't prove it.' It's all one thing she's saying. The pause is just where the 'Mom said' part squeezes in." She read it aloud again, letting her voice run right through the interruption, and both of them heard it: the sentence was still going.

"So write it like it's still going," said Jasraj, who had arrived just in time to steal a corner of Maxwell's muffin. He leaned over the page. "Try a little letter."

Sofia crossed out the capital A and wrote: "I never took your compass," Mom said, "and you can't prove it." She changed the period to a comma too, because the voice in her head hadn't stopped there. It looked strange for a second, and then it looked right. "When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence," she said slowly, writing the rule at the top of her page, "the second part begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing."

"That rule should be on a poster," said Maxwell. "Right next to the muffin menu."

"Rules can't fix everything," Sofia said. "Ms. Moretti also said my story has no climax. It just sort of... drifts." She flipped to her outline, where two characters wandered around a lighthouse arguing about a missing compass and then had dinner.

Jasraj spun her notebook toward himself. "So make the compass turn up somewhere impossible. Inside the lighthouse lantern, maybe. Then whoever finds it has to explain how it got there."

Sofia grinned and started a fresh page. The window circle she had wiped was fogging over again, and she let it, because the argument she was writing next was about to get loud.

"One more hot chocolate," she announced, raising her empty mug toward the counter, "and then the lighthouse thief confesses everything."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: For a metal wire at constant temperature, a graph of voltage against current is a straight line through zero, and its slope is the resistance.
story:
David crouched on the garage floor beside a shoebox of tangled wires, holding a battery like it might bite. "The science fair is Friday," Rhett said from the workbench, where he was supposed to be writing down numbers. "Friday, David. And your project is five scribbles and a hot battery."

"The scribbles are data," David said. He touched the wire clips to a length of copper stretched between two bricks, watched the little meter, and read out, "Point one two volts. Current?" Rhett squinted at the second meter. "Zero point two four amps." He wrote it, then wrote it again because his first zero looked like a six. "This is the part where you tell me what we're actually doing."

David grinned. "We're hunting something invisible." Last summer, he remembered, Mr. Sinclair the neighbour had caught him trying to fix a radio in this same garage and had said, "Electricity is a privilege, not a right, and you've just revoked yours," then handed him a meter and shown him nothing else. Mr. Sinclair believed in making kids find things out the hard way, which at the time had seemed cruel and now seemed like the best afternoon of David's whole summer.

They took five readings, swapping batteries, adjusting a little knob Rhett called "the twiddler" to regulate the current so the meter wouldn't slam to its end. The fifth reading came out near zero, almost nothing, and Rhett groaned. "Great. Zero. Diligent work, team. Zero volts, zero amps, zero project."

"No, wait." David pulled the graph paper toward him and plotted all five points, voltage on one axis, current on the other. The near-zero point sat close to the crossing of the lines, right where the axes met. He lined his ruler up through the rest of them, and the point near zero sat dead on the edge of the ruler's path. "Rhett. Look. Straight line. And it goes through zero."

"So the zero reading was good?" "It was better than good. It's proof." David drew the line firm and dark, then leaned back, chewing his pencil. Mr. Sinclair had said one word back in the summer, just one, and now David understood it. The line climbed, and the steeper it climbed, the more the wire pushed back against the current. He measured the slope, dividing one reading by another, and got half an ohm. He checked a second point on the line. Half an ohm again.

Rhett tapped the paper. "And this slope thing has a name?" David wrote it at the top in block letters. "Resistance," he said, and underlined it twice, so hard the pencil snapped.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
story:
Isabella spread her colored pencils across the kitchen table and glared at the assignment sheet. Two climate graphs, one for a desert and one for a rainforest, due tomorrow morning in Ms. Villanueva's class. She had already drawn the rainforest graph for Manaus, Brazil, where the bars for every single month stacked up tall and green like a crowded fence. The desert graph was the problem. She had chosen the Atacama in Chile because it sounded dramatic, but when she searched for its rainfall numbers, the website showed something strange: some weather stations there had nothing at all where the numbers should have been.

She tapped her pencil against her chin. Maybe the site was broken. She refreshed the page twice, and the empty spaces stayed empty. Then she noticed a small line of text beneath the data table, and read it slowly. Parts of the Atacama were so dry that some weather stations there had never recorded rain. Not a little rain. Not rare rain. None, ever, in the whole time anyone had been measuring. She sat back so fast that her chair squeaked on the floor.

"Manha," she said into her phone, which was propped against the sugar bowl, "your graph for the Sahara still has bars for every month, right?"

"Tiny ones, like little stumps," Manha said. Her face was pixelly but her voice was clear. "Why?"

"Mine doesn't. Some of mine are just missing." Isabella turned her notebook toward the camera so Manha could see the graph she had started, with twelve months along the bottom and only a few short bars drawn in. "I thought I did it wrong. I was going to make up numbers so it would look even."

"Don't you dare make up numbers," Manha said. "Ms. Villanueva can smell a fake graph from across the room."

Isabella laughed, then stopped laughing, because she realized she had almost done exactly that. She had wanted the graph to look complete more than she had wanted it to be true. She picked up her orange pencil instead. "So the missing bars are the point," she said. "A blank month says more than a small one. I'll shade them lightly and label them. That's the whole difference between my desert and your rainforest, right there."

While she shaded, her little brother wandered in and asked for a snack, and his whining about the crackers being "the boring kind" accompanied her quiet concentration like a fly she had learned to ignore. Their mom called from the hallway that the price of crackers had gone up again, thanks to inflation, and that he would survive. Manha suggested, with extravagant enthusiasm, that Isabella add a drawing of a lizard sunbathing beside the desert graph.

"A lizard is not data," Isabella said.

"A lizard is decoration," Manha said. "Data can be beautiful and have a lizard."

Isabella looked at her finished graph, the rainforest one standing beside it like a green mountain range, the desert one flat and half empty in a way that now seemed right. She picked up the orange pencil one more time.

"Fine," she said. "One lizard. But he's going to be holding a tiny umbrella he never gets to use."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
story:
Evelyn crouched at the top of the ramp with a marble in her hand, watching the clock on the lab wall jump from 2:41 to 2:42. Twelve minutes until the bell, and Mr. Nowak had promised the stopwatch cart to the next class the moment it rang.

"Distance is two meters," Kenzi said, marking the finish line with tape. "You roll, I time."

"Then we draw the graph," Evelyn said. "He wants distance on one axis and time on the other." She had never made a graph of anything that moved before. A graph of a ball seemed strange, like drawing a picture of a shout.

They rolled the marble five times. Kenzi called out the times, Evelyn wrote them, and on the sixth run the marble wobbled off the ramp entirely and vanished under the sink. Lex, at the next bench, laughed so hard she knocked over her own stack of meter sticks.

When the bell countdown hit eight minutes, they had their numbers: two meters in 1.6 seconds, again and again, almost exactly. "So the speed is two divided by 1.6," Evelyn muttered, working it out. "One point two five. But of what? Meters per second. What does that even feel like?"

Lex leaned over. "Is that fast? Could your marble beat a person walking?"

"That's the question," Evelyn said. She knew a person walked about five kilometers per hour, but her marble was in meters per second, and the two numbers refused to compare. It was like weighing a backpack in books and her lunch in apples.

Two minutes left. She flipped through her notebook, hunting, and found a half-remembered line in the margin of an old homework page: to change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply by 3.6. She stared at it, then tested it. "One point two five times 3.6 is 4.5," she said. "Four and a half kilometers per hour."

"So the walker wins," Lex said.

"By half a kilometer per hour," Evelyn said, "if the walker keeps a steady pace. Which means our graph should be one straight, steady climb." She plotted the points fast, drew the line, and slid the paper to Kenzi just as Mr. Nowak's hand touched the stopwatch cart.

"Graph of a competent rolling marble," he said, reading the title Evelyn had scrawled. "And what did you infer from your line?"

"The marble lost to a walker," Evelyn said. "But only just."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Michael had typed the last number into column B when Mr. Bekele walked over and said, "Now make it add itself."

"It can do that?" Michael asked.

"Type equals, S-U-M, open parenthesis, B2 colon B9, close parenthesis." Mr. Bekele moved on to Katia, whose screen had gone entirely blue for reasons she was not sharing.

Michael typed it. The number 148 appeared in the cell, which felt like cheating somehow, but he decided not to complain. He was making a chart for the science fair proposal: hours of practice per week for the robotics team versus the chess team. The robotics team had logged 149 hours. The chess team had 148. One hour apart, which was honestly boring.

He clicked Insert Chart, and the bars appeared. The robotics bar towered over the chess bar like a skyscraper over a garden shed.

"Huh," Michael said.

Olivia leaned over from the next computer. "You guys practise way more than us."

"We practise one hour more than you. Total. For the whole week."

"Well, it doesn't look like one hour," Olivia said. "It looks like you double us."

Michael looked at the chart again. The bars, he noticed, didn't start at the floor. The axis along the bottom began at 145, because the software had helpfully chosen that on its own. He clicked on the axis, found the little settings panel, and changed the minimum to zero.

Both bars shot down to nearly the same height. Side by side, they looked like twins.

"Oh," Olivia said. "That's a dirty trick."

"It wasn't on purpose. The program did it." Michael sat back. So the chart could tell the truth and still lie, depending on where the line started. He tried minimum 147, and the gap opened up again, wide as a doorway. At zero, it closed to a crack.

He wrote on his proposal sheet: all charts must start at zero, and made a note that a misleading graph could persuade people who never checked the axis. Somewhere in the school there were probably posters doing exactly this, dormant and unnoticed on hallway walls, waiting for someone like him to catch them.

"Can you do a chart for my data?" Olivia asked. "I counted how many students say 'like' per class period."

"Only if you start at zero."

"You're no fun," Olivia said, but she was smiling.

Mr. Bekele paused behind them, looked at the two near-identical bars, and gave a single approving nod. Michael saved the file twice.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
David pressed his nose against the glass case in the Forces and Motion hall, watching a pendulum swing in slow circles over a ring of sand. "It's drawing a flower," he said. "Every single time. Same flower."

Ophelie leaned in beside him. "So? The sign says the Earth is spinning under it. Big deal."

"But I can't see the Earth spin," David said. "All I can see is the flower in the sand. So my guess is that the pendulum isn't really curving at all, and something hidden is doing it." He pulled his notebook from his back pocket and wrote, fast, so his handwriting came out brittle and spiky across the page. Guess: the floor under the pendulum moves, not the pendulum.

"That's your hypothesis," Ryker said, reading over his shoulder. "My sister does those. It's a guess you can test."

David looked up at the big clock on the wall. Then he did the math on the back of his hand, muttering, and scratched out a little equation to work out how far the floor should slide in ten minutes if his guess was right. "If I mark where the sand flower starts," he said, "and come back in ten minutes, the whole pattern should have turned. If it hasn't turned, my idea is wrong. Dead wrong."

Ryker frowned. "You want to be wrong?"

"No, but listen." David pointed across the hall, where Mr. Ortiz, the demonstrator in the purple vest, was setting up a telescope by the window. "He said something weird at the show this morning. A philosopher named Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong." He said it carefully, the way he'd written it down. "So a real idea has to stick its neck out. Mine is sticking its neck way out."

They marked the sand case with a sticker from Ophelie's folder and ran to the Tesla coil demonstration, which cracked and boomed and made every hair on David's arms stand up. When they raced back, ten minutes and forty seconds later, David skidded to a stop so hard his sneakers squeaked.

The flower had turned. Not much, but turned.

"It moved," Ophelie whispered. "The floor moved. You can't see it and it moved."

David had been so sure the pendulum itself was curving on some invisible breeze from the ceiling vents. He'd even planned to test the vents next. Now he flipped his notebook page over, crossed out his old guess, and wrote a new line under it. "I was wrong about the breeze," he said. "Being wrong is the best thing that's happened all day. What can we test next?"

Ryker tapped the case glass and grinned. "How about why they keep this room so cold?"

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
The poster on the exam room wall depicted two brains side by side, one bright red and one pale blue, with the words STRESS AND WHAT YOUR BODY DOES WITH IT printed underneath. Claire read it three times while she waited for her checkup, mostly because reading anything was better than thinking about Friday's soccer tryouts. She had been thinking about them anyway, all week, at breakfast and in math class and last night at two in the morning, staring at the ceiling.

Mr. Çelik, who ran the office's front desk and sometimes came back to chat with patients, knocked and leaned in. "Still waiting on the doctor. Mind if I hide in here for a minute? The magazine rack out front is a crime scene." He noticed where she was looking. "We just got those posters. A psychologist helped write them. Half the kids who come in here think there's something wrong with them because they worry. There isn't."

Claire pointed at a line near the bottom. "It says fear and anxiety are distinct things. I thought they were the same."

"Read the small print," Mr. Çelik said. "It's a good split."

She read it slowly. Fear was a reaction to a threat happening now, like a dog lunging at you. Anxiety was worry about a threat that might happen in the future, something that hadn't occurred yet. Claire sat back. On Saturday, when a wasp had flown at her face at Alvin's pool party, she had felt a bolt of pure panic that vanished the second the wasp landed on the fence. That had to be fear. But the tryouts were three days away, and nothing bad was happening to her at all, and she still felt sick every morning. She flipped the idea over in her head, testing it. Nobody was growling at her in this room. The threat existed only in her imagination of Friday. So this was anxiety, and anxiety needed different tools than ducking a wasp.

When the doctor came in, Claire asked, before even the usual questions, whether the office had anything about coping with worry. The doctor raised an eyebrow, then pulled a pamphlet from the drawer about stress, breathing, and setting boundaries around things like late-night phone scrolling. "Practicing this week?" the doctor asked, writing the date on it.

"Tryouts Friday," Claire said. "But they haven't happened yet. That's kind of the whole point." She folded the pamphlet into her back pocket and texted Brooks on the way out: not coming over tonight. Starting my tryout worry curfew at eight instead. Brooks sent back a thumbs-up and then, a minute later, a video of Alvin falling into the pool again.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Riley slid two cereal boxes across the kitchen table and gave them his most serious scientist frown. "Santiago, my friend, we are about to settle the biggest question in the history of breakfast."

Santiago dropped into the other chair and peered at the boxes. "Name-brand Crunch-O's, four dollars, versus store-brand Crispy Circles, one fifty. My mom says they're the same thing. My dad says that's a metaphor for something. I stopped listening."

"Here's my problem," Riley said. "Everybody who says they can taste the difference has already seen the box. So which sample are they actually tasting, the cereal or the price?" He tapped the table. "I want to prove it for my science fair project, and I want it to be fair."

Santiago grinned. "So hide the boxes. Pour both cereals into bowls, label one A and one B, and don't tell anybody which is which. Nobody's expectations can sway their answers if they don't know what they're eating." He stood up and went to the cupboard for bowls, then paused. "Wait. Did I just sound smart? Tell no one."

They ran four taste tests that afternoon. Riley's little sister got A and B mixed up twice and accused them of switching bowls, which they had not. Vladimir, recruited by text and lured over with promises of leftover snacks, chewed slowly like a judge on a cooking show and announced, "B is clearly the expensive one. B has a distinct crunch. B has class."

"Which one was B?" Riley asked, keeping his face blank.

"The Crunch-O's, obviously."

It was the store brand. Vladimir stared at his empty bowl as if it had rebelled against everything he believed in. "I have been loyal to that box since kindergarten," he said. "I feel betrayed by myself."

The last tester was Ms. Liu, their neighbor, who came over for the last two bowls. She chose correctly, but when Riley asked her, she shrugged and said, "I guessed. They taste the same to me."

Riley wrote the results in his notebook, then looked at the numbers. Three out of four tasters could not tell the difference once the boxes were hidden. Only one got it right, and she said she'd guessed. He crossed out his old hypothesis, the one that claimed everyone could taste the difference, and wrote a new line.

"Changed my mind," he told Santiago. "People aren't tasting cereal. They're tasting the box."

"Poetic," said Santiago. "Also, we're out of B."

Vladimir was already reaching for the store-brand box.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
The library smelled like pencil shavings and old glue, and Jeremy had three days to learn equations before the retest. He copied a problem from the board photo on his phone: x plus seven equals nineteen. His first instinct was to just guess numbers until one worked, but guessing had already earned him a C-minus and a note home. Konnor slid into the chair across from him with a stack of books about wind power, because Konnor's actual want was the science fair, and the fair was in the same three days.

"If I take seven away from the nineteen, I get twelve," Jeremy said, tapping his pencil. "But how do I know that's not cheating?"

Konnor looked up from a diagram of a turbine. "Maybe look it up. You look everything up." He spun the encyclopedia volume toward Jeremy with one finger, the way a cashier slides change across a counter.

Jeremy needed a source anyway, since Mr. Ahmed had assigned a half-page on the history of a math word. So he typed algebra into the library computer while Konnor, three seats down, muttered about whether his model generator would actually spin or just sit there like a paperweight. The screen loaded slowly, its fan humming like a distant refrigerator. Then Jeremy read the line twice. The word algebra came from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. A thousand and two hundred years ago, someone in Baghdad had been stuck on the same kind of problem, and had written a whole book about it.

"Al-jabr," Jeremy said out loud. "That's where algebra comes from. Some book title."

Konnor raised his thumbs without looking away from his turbine. "Great. Now solve mine: if my blades need to spin at two hundred turns and each gust gives x turns plus forty, find x."

Jeremy wrote x plus forty equals two hundred. He speculated for a second that the rule might be to move numbers around randomly, but that felt like guessing in a costume. Instead he tried one idea and tested it: take forty away from both sides, not just from one. The left became plain x, the right became one hundred sixty, and both sides stayed equal, like a seesaw with matching weights. He tried it on x plus seven equals nineteen. Subtract seven from both sides. x equals twelve. He checked it by putting twelve back in, and twelve plus seven really did equal nineteen.

"It works," Jeremy said. "Both sides. That's the crucial part. You do it to both sides or the whole thing tips over."

Konnor grinned and copied the method onto the back of his wind power notes. Mr. Ahmed passed their table, glanced at Jeremy's page, and slid a sticky note beside the twelfth problem that said only, "Better." Jeremy stuck it to the corner of his notebook like a medal, then wrote his next equation, slow and careful, subtracting eight from both sides.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
The clock on the dashboard said 9:47, and the funeral started at ten thirty, which meant they had exactly forty-three minutes to cross a city that usually took fifty. Romy sat in the back with the plastic bag of Grandpa's things her dad had grabbed from the nursing home: a hairbrush, a paperback western, and a bottle of pills with a prescription label so old the ink had faded to gray. Her little brother was still sniffing into his sleeve. He had announced at breakfast that he was not going to say anything at the funeral, he was just going to hold the western up over his head like a trophy, and nobody had argued with him.

Romy turned the pill bottle over and over. Grandpa had stopped needing it a week before he died, and she wondered whether that meant something, whether the doctors had known. She was skeptical of the whole idea that you could see a death coming in a stack of bottles and brushes, but she kept looking anyway, because looking felt like doing something. Then, without warning, she remembered Aisha's sleepover two nights ago, all four of them screaming with laughter at a movie where a raccoon stole a birthday cake, and her stomach dropped. It had been five days after Grandpa died. Five days. She had laughed so hard she'd wheezed.

"Mom," she said. "Can I ask you something weird?"

Her mom kept her eyes on the road. "Weird is basically all I've got left this week."

"Is it bad that I laughed at Aisha's? Like, does it mean I didn't really love him?"

Her mom was quiet long enough that Romy checked the clock again, 9:51, and then her mom said, "There's a thing two researchers figured out. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, in 1999. It's called the dual process model." She changed lanes, smoothly, like she did this every day. "Grieving people move back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. Back and forth. It's not a straight line through sadness. It's a zigzag."

Romy watched the hospital sign go past where Grandpa had stayed. So the laughing wasn't a betrayal; it was the other side of the zigzag, the daily-life side, and her brain had been doing exactly what brains were built to do. She could almost see it, a path switching between two rooms. "So tonight I might be sad again and that's normal too?"

"That's the whole model," her mom said.

That was when Romy noticed the sound she'd been hearing since they got in the car. She'd assumed her mom was crying, because today that made sense, but her mom's shoulders were shaking differently. She was laughing, silently, at something.

"What? What is it?"

Her mom pointed at the radio, which had been playing Grandpa's favorite station the whole drive. "That song. It was playing the night your grandfather tried to convert our garage into a chicken coop. He played it eleven times in a row. Eleven." A tear ran down her cheek while she was still grinning. "Zigzag," she said.

Her brother unbuckled, leaned between the seats, and held the western up. "Ten twenty-six. We can still make it if Dad runs the yellow."

"Watch this," said her dad, and pressed the gas.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
Lauren's kitchen smelled like garlic and ambition, which was her way of saying she had a plan. "The school cooking contest is in two weeks," she announced, pulling a cutting board from the cupboard, "and my sauce is going to win. You're helping, because you have steady hands and I need a witness."

Nathaniel set the onion on the board and picked up the knife the way she'd shown him, fingers curled under so his knuckles guided the blade. "Claw grip," he said, mostly to remind himself. "If I lose a fingertip, I'm telling Ms. Tanaka it was your fault." Lauren rolled her eyes and handed him a paper towel for the tears that were coming.

The first cut went fine. The second one did not. The board skated sideways across the counter the moment he pressed down, and the knife skipped off the onion and clattered onto the counter a terrifying inch from his thumb. "Okay," he said, standing very still. "The board moved. Not me. The board."

"It always does that," Lauren said, peering into the fridge. "It's like it's trying to escape. My little brother calls it the runaway board. He's basically a parasite who lives in my house and eats my snacks, and even he noticed."

Nathaniel stared at the board. It hadn't moved when he'd just set the onion down. It moved when he pushed down on it. So something about the pressure was letting it slide, which meant the fix might be stopping the slide, not stopping the push. Last summer at his grandmother's house, he suddenly remembered, she had laid a wet dish towel under her ancient wooden board before chopping herbs all afternoon, and it had never budged. He'd thought it was just one of her odd habits, like talking to her tomato plants, who she claimed were the only good listeners in the family.

"Give me a paper towel," he said, and ran it under the tap until it was damp, then spread it flat on the counter and set the board on top. He pressed down. The board stayed put, firm as a sidewalk. He pressed harder. Nothing. "Ha! Damp paper towel under the cutting board. It stops the board from sliding while you chop."

"Grandma trick," Lauren said approvingly. "Okay, claws up. Medium dice, and don't rush, because last time you rushed, we both remember the garlic incident."

He chopped. His eyes streamed and his forehead began to perspire, and Lauren laughed so hard she had to sit on a stool, but the cuts came out even, and the pile of onion grew neat and square-edged. They dumped it into the pot with olive oil, and the kitchen filled with a hiss and a smell that made even the parasite wander in from the living room to investigate.

"Careful," Lauren said, pointing at the splattering sauce. "It's hot oil and it's flammable, so no leaning over the pot like a curious giraffe." Nathaniel stirred, added the tomatoes, and tasted from the wooden spoon she held out. The sauce was tangy and a little sweet, and he felt a grin spreading across his face. Lauren grabbed a second spoon, tasted it, and thrust her fist in the air. "First place," she declared. "Two weeks of practice, and it starts with this."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
story:
James twisted the fine focus knob so hard that the whole microscope shuddered, and still the eyepiece showed him nothing but a pale gray fog. "My onion cells are invisible," he announced. "I have ghost cells."

"Let me guess," said Adrienne, leaning over from the next station. "You clicked straight to the big lens, the one that says forty times on it."

"So? Big lens, big view. That's just math."

Adrienne snorted. "You're using the strongest lens to hunt for something you haven't even found yet. That's like using binoculars to find your socks."

Ms. Walker drifted past their benches, hands behind her back, radiating the calm of someone who had watched a hundred kids fight the same microscope. "How's it going, scientists?"

"My cells are ghosts," James said.

"Hmm," said Ms. Walker, and kept walking, which James felt was unhelpful, though also possibly a clue.

He sat back and stared at the little disc of onion skin he'd peeled off with tweezers, so thin it was nearly see-through. He thought about the binoculars. Cale, across the aisle, was already happily sketching what looked like a brick wall made of blobs, and Cale was not what anyone would call an exceptional science student. James was, or at least he'd told his grandmother he was. So how had Cale found cells that James couldn't?

His instinct said: copy whatever Cale did, but pretend you thought of it yourself. He stood up, wandered past Cale's bench, and glanced down. Cale's microscope was clicked to the smallest lens, the one labeled with the smallest number. Then Cale had flipped to a bigger one and kept sketching.

Huh.

James went back to his station. He clicked the turret all the way around to the shortest lens, the low-power one, and pressed his eye to the eyepiece. At first there was only brightness, but when he turned the knob slowly, shapes swam up out of the fog: rows and rows of rounded boxes, like a honeycomb that had been squashed flat. The onion cells. Not ghosts at all, just very small and very lost until now.

"Found them!" he shouted, then lowered his voice. "Found them," he whispered.

"Wasn't that hard," Cale called over.

James ignored him. With the cells centered, he clicked up to the next lens, and there they were again, bigger and sharper, like the honeycomb had leaned in close. A dark dot sat inside each box. He grabbed his worksheet and started labeling: cell wall, the boxy outline; cell membrane, pressed just inside it; nucleus, the dot.

He drew the last label, then held his pencil up like a tiny trophy. "Adrienne," he said, "you may now admire my exceptional cells."

Adrienne looked over. "Half your labels are on the air bubbles."

James peered into the eyepiece. "Those," he said, "are my ghost cells' swimming pool."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
The bleachers in the Farley Middle gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and Louis was supposed to be watching the game. Instead he had Anders's laptop open on his knees, scrutinizing two columns of numbers he'd found on a baseball stats site. "You're going to miss the tip-off," said Fateh, who was saving seats for them and taking the job seriously.

"I need to settle something first," Louis said. He'd made a bet with his older cousin last summer that Derek Jeter was the better hitter, and the cousin had laughed and said to look it up. Louis had put it off for months. Now, on the bus ride to the game, Anders had bet him a slice of pizza that David Justice beat Jeter both seasons. On the screen the numbers sat there being impossible. "Justice's average is higher in 1995. Justice again in 1996. Both years. He wins twice."

"Then he's better," Anders said. "Two out of two."

"Except look." Louis turned the laptop so both boys could see. "Add the years together, and Jeter's combined average is higher. Justice wins each year and loses overall." The buzzer sounded, the crowd roared, and none of them looked up.

During halftime Louis texted his cousin: I owe you an apology and a slice of pizza. Justice beat Jeter in '95 and in '96, but Jeter's two-year combined average is higher. I thought one number would settle it. The reply came back a minute later: smart kid. now watch your game.

So he did. Farley was down by six, and the scoreboard also ran a news ticker along its bottom edge, headlines about a random lottery winner and about the recession dragging on in some state far away. Louis stared at the screen and thought about how the whole year of a country had been squeezed into that one gray word, recession, the same way a whole season of hitting got squeezed into a single number. He had spent half a year defending Jeter without checking anything, and he'd been wrong about why he was right. Or maybe right about being wrong. He couldn't quite sort it out, and he decided that was okay.

In the fourth quarter Fateh stood up, screaming, as Farley's point guard stole the ball and drove the length of the floor. Louis stood up too, still holding the phone with his cousin's message on it. "Next season," he shouted over the noise, "I'm checking everything twice." The point guard laid the ball in off the glass, and the gym shook.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
Brooke stood at the edge of the reception hall holding a wrapped box of fancy soap, which was the gift her mother had chosen, and watched the French side of the family arrive. Aunt Céline came first, kissed Brooke twice on the cheeks, once on each side. Then Uncle Marc arrived, and he kissed her three times, cheek, cheek, and cheek again, so that Brooke had to rock back on her heels to keep from tipping over. She was sure she had counted right, and the two counts contradicted each other, which bothered her the way a wrong answer on a quiz bothered her. She wanted to get this right before the toasts, because she was supposed to greet the bride's grandmother too.

Ophelia slid up beside her with a cup of punch. "Your relatives are very kissy."

"They do la bise," Brooke said, using the word her cousin Lyna had taught her on the drive over. "Cheek kisses. But I can't figure out the number." She pulled Ophelia behind the dessert table, which had a white cloth that reached the floor and made a decent hiding spot, and they watched. Aunt Céline greeted Lyna with two kisses. Uncle Marc greeted Lyna with three. Then a second aunt arrived, one from Lyon, and she gave Lyna three kisses as well. Brooke kept count on her fingers inside her pocket. Two from the ones who lived in Paris. Three from the ones who came from somewhere else in France.

"Maybe it's where they're from," Ophelia whispered. "Like accents."

It was a testable idea, and Brooke liked those. When Lyna wandered over to steal a strawberry, Brooke asked her, quietly, "Does everybody from your city do three, and everybody from Paris do two?"

Lyna nodded like it was the most ordinary thing in the world. "It changes from region to region. You'll get mixed up if you try to memorize us all. Even I do, and we're basically a kissing dynasty at this point."

The bride's grandmother was small and quick, and she arrived at the dessert table before Brooke had planned her approach. There was no time to wonder which city the grandmother was from. Brooke offered her hand, since that was what she did at home, but the grandmother leaned in and waited, cheeks ready, until Brooke understood and gave two kisses, because the grandmother had married into the Paris side, and Paris, as far as Brooke's data showed, was a two-kiss city. The grandmother beamed and said something warm that Brooke didn't understand a word of.

At dinner, Uncle Marc told a long story about the bride as a girl, and everyone laughed, and then the cake came out, and Lyna leaned over and whispered, "You did the bise perfectly, by the way. Grand-mère doesn't kiss just anyone twice." Brooke sat up straighter and reached for her fork, using the outside one first, the way the French cousins did.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
The handwritten sign taped to the gas station's drink cooler said two dollars a bottle, but Carter had paid one dollar for the same lemonade on Tuesday. Behind the counter, Mr. Gauthier was crossing out numbers on a clipboard like he was solving a puzzle he kept losing. Outside, the sky had gone the color of wet slate, and the radio behind the register repeated the words storm warning in between bursts of static.

"Thirsty people pay more when there's less of something," Mr. Gauthier said when Carter asked about the sign. He jerked his thumb toward the shelf of umbrellas by the door, marked down to three dollars from twelve. "Nobody wants those on a sunny day. Want to know what I do all afternoon? I move prices up and down until everything sells out exactly, no leftovers, no empty shelf either."

Carter turned that over while he counted the lemonade bottles. There were nine left. At two dollars, people had taken six in the last hour. He pulled out his phone and typed a message to Johanna: "Watching Mr. Gauthier change prices all afternoon. I think there's one magic number for everything in the store. Testing it now. If the storm knocks out power, batteries should go up before they run out. Umbrellas should go down. Watch."

Her reply came in under a minute, assertive as always: "You're on. If you're right, buy me the kangaroo keychain by the register. Its pouch is supposed to symbolize carrying luck, and I need luck before my soccer tryout." The keychain was a fat little gray marsupial dangling beside the lottery tickets, and its price tag said four dollars, the same as it had all summer.

By six o'clock the storm was close enough that the streetlights flickered. Mr. Gauthier raised the batteries to eight dollars, and the last pack sold just as he flipped the sign to CLOSED. The umbrellas went to a dollar and vanished. The lemonade found its number at three dollars, and the ninth bottle walked out the door in a delivery driver's hand at exactly closing time. Nothing left over. Nothing left behind.

Carter stood in the doorway while the first rain hammered the pavement. Adrian came splashing across the lot with his hood up, staring at the darkened shelves through the glass. "How did every single thing sell out right at closing?" he asked. Carter grinned and held up the little kangaroo. "Johanna says when the amount buyers want equals the amount the seller has, that's called the equilibrium price. Mr. Gauthier found it all day. Also, I owe this to her by morning."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
Evelyn had stayed after the final bell because Mr. Qureshi kept a jar of balance scales on his desk, little brass weights she used to calibrate her guesses until they matched. That was how she had learned to solve equations: take away three from the left pan, take away three from the right, and the scale stays even. She was getting good at it, good enough that Mr. Qureshi had pinned her last quiz on the wall beside the window where the monsoon rain streaked the glass.

"You look lethargic today," she told Lennox, who sat slumped at the next desk with his pencil barely moving. Outside, the rain drummed on the portico roof, and the whole classroom smelled like wet sneakers.

"I've been on this one since lunch," Lennox said. He slid his paper toward her. At the top, in Mr. Qureshi's looping handwriting, it said: x + 1 = x + 2. Below it, Lennox had filled half a page. He had tried x equals one, then two, then five, then twelve, then a messy row of crossed-out fractions. "Every time I check it, it's wrong. Every single time."

Evelyn set up the brass weights. One unknown block plus one small weight on the left pan, the same unknown block plus two small weights on the right. Then she did what she always did, the same operation to both sides: she lifted the unknown block off the left pan and lifted the matching block off the right. The scale should have stayed even, the way it always did.

It didn't. One small weight sat alone on the left, two on the right, and the beam tipped hard. She took one small weight from each side next, and still it tipped: nothing on the left, one weight on the right, and nothing she could remove would fix it.

"Wait," she said. "Try x equals zero."

Lennox plugged it in. "Zero plus one is one. Zero plus two is two. One doesn't equal two." He tried it with his fraction, then with twelve again. "It's never equal. Not for anything."

"It can't be," Evelyn said slowly, watching the beam sit crooked. "No number is one more and two more than itself at once." She picked up the small brass weight from the right pan and held it in her palm. "You weren't getting it wrong. There's no answer to get."

Lennox stared at his half page of work, then laughed so suddenly that Ismael, sweeping paper scraps by the door, looked over. "So the answer is that there isn't one?"

"There has to be a way to write that," Evelyn said, and she was already copying the puzzle onto a fresh sheet.

Mr. Qureshi came in from the rain, shaking water off his jacket, and set his bag on the desk between them. He looked at the crooked scale, then at their faces.

"Ah," he said. "You found one of mine."

"Is that allowed?" Lennox asked. "A problem with no solution?"

Mr. Qureshi smiled and pulled a chair around. "Show me how you know."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Anna had ten minutes to draw a labeled onion cell before the bell, and so far all she had drawn was a gray circle of nothing. The microscope's light glowed up at her like a tiny sun, but the slide itself stayed black. She had cut a chunk of onion from her lunch sandwich that morning, a thick, juicy slab, and pressed it under the cover slip like a specimen in a nature documentary.

"Move over," said Youcef, bumping her elbow. "You're not going to see anything through that thing. It's like trying to shine a flashlight through a tsunami of onion." He held up his own slide, which showed a clean brick-wall pattern of cells, each one with its nucleus floating like a dark pearl.

"Then why is yours working?" Anna said, and immediately wished she hadn't, because Youcef grinned like a fox who had found the henhouse unlocked.

Madina leaned between them, smelling sharply of onion juice. "Because Mr. Bighorn was frugal with his supplies and only gave us one razor blade each, that's why. He made me peel off the papery outside and take the thin skin from inside the ring. Look how thin it is. You can almost see through it."

Anna held Madina's scrap of onion skin up to the ceiling light, and it was like holding a ghost. The light came straight through it. Her thick chunk, she realized, was like a wall; light could not get past it, so the microscope had nothing to show her. The thin skin had to be practically see-through for the scope to work, maybe only one cell deep. That would explain everything. It would also explain why Mr. Bighorn kept saying "one cell thick" in that annoying sing-song voice while sharpening pencils at his desk.

She peeled her chunk apart, hunting for the inner skin, the thin film that clings between the layers. Her fingers smelled like a salad bar. "If I get this," she announced, "Youcef owes me his gummy worm."

"Deal," said Youcef. "And if you fail, you owe me your tsunami of onion."

Anna laid the whisper-thin film on a fresh slide, dropped the cover slip, and squinted. The gray nothing bloomed into bricks, clear cell walls boxing in each cell, a dark nucleus at the center like a tiny button. She drew fast, labeling wall, membrane, nucleus, her pencil scratching as the clock ticked. When the bell rang she held up her paper, sticky-fingered and triumphant, and Youcef sadly surrendered the gummy worm.

"Careful," Madina said, watching Anna dangle it over her mouth. "That thing's been in your pocket since Tuesday. It could hibernate for the winter."

Anna examined it, shrugged, and ate it anyway.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Leave No Trace outdoor ethics are organized as seven principles, including 'dispose of waste properly' and 'leave what you find'.
story:
The diner's neon sign said EAT, and William's stomach agreed. His family had been driving since sunrise toward Pine Canyon National Park, and now they were squeezed into a booth by the window, waiting for pancakes, when he heard a familiar voice yell his name. Lauren from his class was three booths over with her own family, wearing the same stunned look he probably had.

"Small world," Lauren said, sliding into the seat beside him. Her parents had taken a different highway and still ended up here. "Guess where we're going. Pine Canyon. Same as you."

"You should carpool," William's dad said, and everybody laughed, even the tired waitress.

Lauren pulled a folded park brochure from her jacket and smoothed it flat between the syrup dispensers. "My mom made me memorize the rules before we get there," she groaned. "She's systematic about it. Charts on the fridge, a checklist, the whole thing." William leaned over. The brochure had a list with a bold heading: Leave No Trace. Below it were seven principles, numbered one through seven. He read them while their food arrived. Number three said "dispose of waste properly," which seemed obvious, trash goes in a bin, fine. But number four stopped him: "leave what you find."

"No fair," he said. "I was going to bring home one of those striped rocks from the canyon floor. The orange ones with the white bands."

"You can't," Lauren said, tapping the page. "It's right there."

William wasn't convinced by a piece of paper. A single rock, he reasoned, couldn't matter; nobody would even notice a gap. So on their first morning in the park, he decided to test the idea. He picked up a striped rock, set it on a flat stretch of trail, and walked ten steps away to watch. Within two minutes a little girl crouched over it, gasped, showed her brother, and carefully put it back exactly where it had been, patting the dirt around it like it was a sleeping pet. Then a photographer knelt and took a picture of the same spot. William stood there feeling like he'd witnessed something invisible, a chain of people who each wanted that rock to stay.

At the next diner, on the drive home, he found Lauren's family in the parking lot. "I get it now," he said, holding up nothing but his phone, which showed the photo the photographer had let him copy. "If everyone took one, there'd be none left. That's the concept, right? Leave what you find." Lauren nodded solemnly, then ruined it by grinning. "I'm going to petition my mom for pie," she announced. "Coming?"

"Race you to the counter," William said.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
story:
Rosalie sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her Spanish notebook open and her dog, Nutmeg, asleep against her knee. The assignment was due tomorrow: describe your family and pets in full sentences, out loud, no English allowed. She had written "Tengo un perro" and "Mi madre es profesora," and she was halfway through "Tengo dos hermanos" when her tablet buzzed. It was April, calling from her kitchen.

"Are you watching the practice videos Ms. Baptiste posted?" April said. "Because there's something weird in the third one. The girl says 'Tengo dos hermanos,' and I thought, okay, two brothers, but then she holds up a picture and it's one boy and one girl. A brother and a sister. That's not two brothers. Did she mess up her own video?"

Rosalie scrolled to the third video and watched it twice. The girl said the sentence clearly, no hesitation, and the picture definitely showed a boy and a girl. "She didn't stumble," Rosalie said slowly. "It sounded like something she'd said a hundred times. So maybe it's not a mistake. Maybe it's a rule we just haven't hit yet." She paused, wondering. "Like, what if one word can cover both? That would be a weird shortcut, but languages love shortcuts."

"Or she's a volatile person who changes her mind about her siblings," April said, and Rosalie laughed so hard Nutmeg woke up and barked at the tablet.

"We can't eliminate either theory without more evidence," Rosalie said. "Witnesses. We're basically detectives. Hang on." She put the call on speaker, ran downstairs, and knocked on Ms. Baptiste's door across the hall, since her neighbor had grown up speaking Spanish and was always offering to quiz her. "Ms. Baptiste, if someone has one brother and one sister, and they say 'Tengo dos hermanos,' is that wrong?"

Ms. Baptiste smiled. "No, that's exactly right. 'Hermanos' means brothers, or brothers and sisters together."

Rosalie raced back upstairs, breathless. "It's real! The girl in the video was telling the truth. You can say one word and it covers both." She opened her notebook and crossed out nothing, because her sentence was suddenly perfect. On the tablet, April was already muttering her own version under her breath, and Benedict had joined the call, demanding to know what they'd figured out without him.
