"You're the last defendant to hear the verdict," April told him. "Hermanos is sneakier than it looks."

"Then watch this," Rosalie said, and held the tablet up so the camera caught Nutmeg, still grumbling from the bark. "Tengo un perro," she said, clear and steady, and Nutmeg licked the screen.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Buddhism teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul, called anatta or no-self, so what continues from life to life is a chain of karma, not an unchanging self.
story:
Luca spread his notes across the kitchen table like a general planning a battle. On one side, a page labeled "Hinduism" in his best printing; on the other, a page labeled "Buddhism," still half blank. The assignment was due Monday, and Mr. Rosen had said the trick was comparing the two religions' ideas about what happens after death, not just describing each one separately.

Ishaan arrived at ten with his backpack and a bag of chips, because he claimed studying required snacks. "Okay," he said, dropping into the chair beside Luca, "so my grandmother says in Hinduism the soul, the atman, gets reborn again and again until it finally reaches moksha, which is like freedom." He tapped Luca's Hinduism page. "Same soul, new body. It's the same you, moving from life to life."

Luca wrote that down, then frowned at the Buddhism page. "But I kept reading that Buddhism says rebirth too, and I thought it was the same thing." He flipped through his library book, skimming lines about karma. Something snagged in his mind, the way a thread catches on a nail. "Wait. It can't be the same thing, or my pages would match and the assignment would be pointless."

Ishaan leaned over and read aloud, slower and slower, until he stopped at a single word printed in bold. "Anatta," he said. "It means no-self." Luca grabbed his pencil. Buddhism taught rebirth but denied a permanent soul, so what continued from one life to the next wasn't an unchanging self at all. It was karma, a chain of cause and effect passing along like one flame lighting the next candle. "That's the difference we missed!" Luca said, half standing, his knee banging the table. "Both have rebirth, but one says a soul travels, and one says there's no permanent soul, just karma carrying on."

Just then his phone buzzed with a message from Raphael, who was stuck at his cousin's birthday party and desperate for help: "Did you figure out the afterlife thing? I only have a paragraph about recycling. NOT the same thing, I know." Luca laughed out loud and typed back: "Hinduism: soul reborn. Buddhism: rebirth but no permanent soul, anatta, only karma continues. Write it exactly like that." Raphael sent back a row of exclamation marks.

They worked until noon, and when Luca's mom came in to make lunch, she asked if the two of them had been arguing. "Not arguing," Luca said. "Discovering." He held up his chart, two columns now filled to the bottom, and slid it across the table toward her. "Read this and tell me which side sounds like a detective story."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
Muhammad had wanted to be on the blue team all afternoon, and he could not figure out why. Alice's birthday party had split into two teams for a scavenger hunt after Alice's dad drew names out of a bowl, and within an hour the reds and blues were chanting at each other across the backyard like they had been enemies for years. It was just a bowl. Just folded slips of paper.

"Clarify something for me," Muhammad said, crouching beside Alice near the garden wall, where a patch of orange lichen spread across the bricks like spilled paint. "Did anyone tell us to act like this?"

"Act like what?" Alice said. She was checking her list, which said lichen, bottle cap, feather, something blue.

"Like the blue team matters. I've never even met half the blue team. Denver's on it, but the others are from Alice's school, not ours." He peeled his eyes away from the wall. "I cheered when a red kid dropped his feather. I don't even know his name."

Alice paused. "You did kind of yell."

Muhammad tested an idea. At the snack table he found Denver, who was on the blue team, and asked him straight out whether they should trade his feather for a red teammate's feather, even up, since both were worth the same points. Denver stared at him like he'd suggested selling his own shoes. "Why would I help red?"

"It's worth the same. It's a feather, Denver."

"Blue found it," Denver said, and that was that.

So Muhammad tried the reverse. He took his own blue slip to Alice's dad and asked to be put on the red team, just for the rest of the hunt. Alice's dad laughed and said switching wasn't allowed, the teams were set. Muhammad went back to the wall and thought. A bowl had picked the teams, randomly, and yet everyone was acting like the bowl had chosen sides that meant something. When he was blue, he had felt blue mattered. He hadn't felt it before the bowl. That was the pattern, and it fit every person in the yard.

He stood up. "Listen," he called out. "Alice's dad picked the teams out of a bowl. Randomly. Nobody's actually anything. We're all just whatever slip we pulled."

The yard went quiet for a second. Then a red kid said, "Blue still stinks," and everybody laughed, the kind of laugh where nobody quite means it anymore. Alice's dad announced that the last item, mandatory for both teams, would be found only if they combined lists, since he'd hidden one half with the red clues and one half with the blues.

They found the birthday cake hiding spot together, all twelve of them squished behind the garage. "Blue stinks," Denver whispered to Muhammad, grinning, and handed him the first slice.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
story:
The park track smelled like cut grass and somebody's burnt hot dogs, and Stella was standing at the eight-hundred-metre start line wondering why she had signed up for the county meet at all. The coach had said it was prestigious, which apparently meant the finish line had a banner and a lady with a clipboard. Stella's plan for the first race of her life had been simple: run fast, then keep running fast. That plan had died in her first practice time trial, when she'd sprinted the first lap like a startled rabbit and then spent the second lap walking with her hands on her head while Livia jogged past her twice, or at least it felt like twice.

"Pace the first lap," Ms. Sok had said, tapping her watch. "Save something." Stella had nodded, but pacing felt like a mysterious talent other people were born with, like whistling or cartwheels.

The wind came across the back straight in long, steady shoves, rattling the flags on the infield. During the second heat, Stella stood at the fence beside Livia and Jolie, watching a girl from Riverside with a green headband take the lead. The girl in second place, a small kid from another school, ran almost close enough to step on Green Headband's heels, tucked in behind her the whole way down the back straight, then swung out at the last bend and beat her by four strides. Livia squinted at the scoreboard. "She looked like she was hiding back there."

Stella watched the third heat, and the fourth, monitoring the back straight each time the wind gusted. When two runners went out single file, the one behind almost always had something left at the end. When they ran side by side, both of them faded on the last lap, arms pumping, faces crumpling like wet paper. It was a pattern, and Stella had a guess about it. Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, she thought, so following someone can save energy for the finish. It wasn't the sort of thing she could see, exactly. She was inferring it from four races and a lot of crumpled faces.

She found Jolie at the snack table, where the booster club was counting the revenue from muffin sales into a shoebox. "I need you to hold the stopwatch and watch me on the back straight," Stella said. "Tell me if I tuck in or not, and what my legs look like at the end."

In her heat, the wind was worse than ever, flapping the number pinned to her back. Stella went out in third, and when the leader swung wide on the back straight, Stella slid in behind her, close enough to see the stitching on her shoulder. The wind that had been leaning on Stella for eighty metres just... stopped leaning. It hit the girl in front instead. Stella stayed there the whole straight, then the bend, then the second lap, and with a hundred metres left her legs still felt like legs and not like two wet towels. She passed one runner. She passed two.

She came second, and Ms. Sok didn't even look at her watch.

"You hid," Jolie said at the fence, grinning. "Behind that girl. The whole back straight."

"I know," Stella said, still catching her breath. "Best spot on the track."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Chase crouched over the patio table with a pencil, a ruler, and a drawing of a street that looked like it had been squashed by a truck. "The road's supposed to go back," he muttered. "Not up."

April leaned over his shoulder. "It looks like a ramp to the moon."

"That's the problem." He flipped his pencil sideways. "Ms. Wright said something today about a vanishing point, and I only half heard it."

Charlene dropped onto the bench across from him. "I heard all of it," she said. "Remember the print she hung by the window? The old fresco from Florence. Masaccio's Holy Trinity, painted around 1427." She grabbed his ruler and laid it flat on the table. "She said it's one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point."

Chase sat up. "The one with the arches and the ceiling?"

"That's the one."

He remembered the field trip to the gallery last fall, how he'd stood in front of that same print while April traced the ceiling lines with her finger, dragging her fingertip along each beam until her hand stopped at one spot in the middle of the page. "They all meet here," she'd said. "Every single one." At the time he'd thought it was a weird game. Now his stomach jumped. The beams weren't just angled for fun. Something invisible was running the whole picture.

He yanked his sketchbook toward him and started over. One dot in the middle of the page. Then the road: two lines running from the bottom corners straight to the dot. The buildings, the sidewalk cracks, the roofline, all of them aimed at that same point like they were tied to it with string. His pencil kept stopping, and each time it stopped, the line landed on the dot.

"Whoa," April said. "It looks real."

"It looks authentic," Charlene said, holding it up to the light. "Like a photograph of a street."

Chase's hand was shaking a little, but in a good way. He thought about every street he'd ever walked down, how the buildings seemed to lean toward each other far away even though he knew they stood straight and parallel. The lines weren't really meeting. Something about the distance made them look that way, and now his paper proved it.

He tested the idea anyway, because he wanted to be sure. He drew a window on the left building and aimed its top and bottom edges at the dot too. Then he drew one on the right, same thing. He sat back. Every window on every wall pointed home to that one spot.

"I'm doing the whole street," he said, already sharpening his pencil. "Streetlights, mailboxes, everything."

April grinned. "This is going to cause a controversy at school. Nobody else's looks like this."

"Exactly." Chase pressed his pencil to the paper and drew the first streetlight, its pole leaning gently toward the dot.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The comment appeared under Mila's photo of her watercolor sunset, posted to the class art page. "This is so ugly, why do you even try," it said, and the username was Skye's. Mila read it three times, because Skye had sat beside her in art yesterday, complimenting the exact same painting in a soft, careful voice. At lunch Skye had even saved her the last orange.

At school the next morning, Skye was polite as always. She held the door for Amal, asked Ms. Weber about the homework in a cheerful chirp, and waved at Mila across the hallway. Mila waved back and felt like she was waving at two different people. The one on the screen and the one in the hallway could not be the same girl, could they?

In the library, Mila typed "why are people mean online but nice in person" into the search bar. She found a page about a psychologist named John Suler who, in 2004, described something he called the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. She copied the words into her notebook, then tested her idea against the evidence like Ms. Weber had taught them in science. Public hallway: nice Skye. Private bedroom, phone in hand, no faces to see: mean Skye. The pattern fit.

"So you saw it too?" Amal whispered when Mila showed him the comment at lunch. His sandwich froze halfway to his mouth. Amal had gotten a message from Skye last week, something extravagant and cutting about his shoes, and he had assumed she hated him. "I almost stopped eating lunch with you guys," he admitted. "I figured she was only nice when teachers could enforce the rules."

"She's nice everywhere except the screen," Mila said. "That's the whole signal I keep missing." She looked down the table at Skye, who was laughing at something, her whole face open and warm. Mila decided not to reply in the comments, where everyone could watch the fight like a show. Instead, that night, she wrote a private message.

"Hey Skye. You said something mean under my painting. I'm not mad, I'm just confused, because you complimented it in person yesterday. Can we talk at school? I'll bring the orange."

She set the phone face down on her desk and stared at the ceiling, her heart tapping like a woodpecker. The reply came before she could count to ten.

Mila picked up the phone. "I'm sorry," the message read. "It's easier to be awful when I can't see anyone's face. Bring two oranges?"

Mila smiled and typed back one word. "Three."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms or trouble falling asleep.
story:
The morning of the canoe regatta, Anthony's stomach hurt so badly he skipped the nutritious breakfast of eggs and toast that Ms. Oliveira had made for the whole cabin. "Too nervous to eat?" she asked, and he shook his head, because he wasn't nervous. He just felt sick.

It had started two nights ago. Darcy had mentioned, casually, that the regatta was the biggest race of the summer, with the camp director watching from the dock. That night Anthony lay awake for hours, listening to Evander snore above him. The next morning his head ached and his palms were so sweaty the paddle nearly slipped. He told no one. He was team captain, and captains didn't fall apart.

He found Darcy at the water's edge, counting life vests. "Have you ever had a stomachache before something big?" he asked, trying to sound like he was just curious.

"Every Sunday night before Monday spelling tests," Darcy said. "My mom took me to the pharmacist once, and the pharmacist asked if anything big happens at school on Mondays. That's when we figured it out." She looked at him sideways. "Why?"

Anthony opened his mouth to say no reason, but his stomach twisted again, sharp enough to make him wince. "It's nothing," he said. "I think I ate a bad hot dog."

The first heat started in twenty minutes. Anthony sat on a rock and thought it through like a math problem. Bad hot dogs don't come back three days in a row. Bad hot dogs don't give you sweaty palms. Darcy's stomachaches came before spelling tests, which meant they were about the test, not about food. His own stomachaches had started the moment Darcy mentioned the director watching from the dock. There was a pattern, and the pattern pointed at something he couldn't see: the race was intimidating him, and his body was doing the talking.

"So it's stress," Darcy said, when he finally admitted it. "My brother gets headaches from it. My mom says it can mess up your sleep, too."

"That's the part I hate," Anthony said. "I haven't slept since Tuesday."

Darcy held up a hand. "Breathe with me. In for four, out for four. My swim coach taught me before finals." They sat on the rock, breathing together while the crowd gathered at the dock. In for four, out for four. The knot in his stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a fist unclenching.

"Ten minutes!" Evander shouted, dragging their canoe toward the water.

"One more thing," Darcy said. "Tonight, no flashlight, no whispering with Evander. Just bed. Trust me."

Anthony picked up his paddle, and his palms, for the first time in three days, were dry. "Ready," he called back across the sand.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
Vincent stood in front of the bathroom mirror holding his arms away from his body like a scarecrow. The shirt he had worn for one hour already showed two dark ovals under the arms, and no matter how he angled himself in the light, they refused to disappear. This had started a few weeks ago, somewhere between his birthday and now, and it annoyed him the way a dripping faucet annoys you at night: small, constant, impossible to ignore.

On the counter sat a stick of deodorant his mom had bought him. He had been swiping it on every morning, yet the ovals kept coming back, sometimes worse than before. That was the part that puzzled him. He leaned closer to the label, reading the small print. The word deodorant was there, but so was another word he had skipped over: antiperspirant. The two sounded almost the same, like cousins, but the label on his stick mentioned nothing about wetness. He turned the stick over twice, as if flipping it might reveal a hidden paragraph. He wanted to diagnose the problem properly instead of guessing, because guessing had gotten him two weeks of sweaty shirts.

That evening he found a note folded on his pillow, in Juniper's handwriting, because she had been over that afternoon and had noticed him holding his arms weird. "Dear Vincent," it read. "I asked my older brother about your armpit situation since you won't. He says deodorants do not stop sweat, they only reduce or cover the smell. Antiperspirants are the opposite: they reduce the sweating itself. So your stick is fighting the smell and losing the wetness battle. Check the store labels. Also, you still owe me a granola bar. Sincerely, Juniper."

The next day Vincent rode his bike to the pharmacy and planted himself in the aisle like a scientist in a lab. Product after product, label after label. The deodorants made claims about freshness and scent. The ones marked antiperspirant said, in distinct lettering, that they reduced sweat, and one line explained how: by temporarily plugging the sweat ducts. He read it twice. Plugging the ducts. It was strange to think about pipes inside his own skin, tiny ones, doing all this. He picked the antiperspirant, paid with crumpled bills, and pedaled home fast enough to work up a test sweat.

The twist came that evening when Rehan came over and sniffed the air suspiciously. "Did you switch soaps or something? You smell different." Vincent laughed and told him about the labels. "Wait," Rehan said. "So my dad's been buying the wrong thing for years?" They looked up the label on the stick in Rehan's bathroom cabinet, and sure enough, plain deodorant, no sweat stopping at all. "I'm texting him," Rehan said, already typing.

The following Monday, Vincent wore his light gray shirt, the one he had banned from his closet, and kept his arms at his sides all through class. At lunch he checked quietly in the boys' room mirror. Dry. He grinned at his reflection and whispered, "Plugged."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A Presta valve has a small nut on top that must be unscrewed before any air can be pumped in or let out.
story:
Everly knelt on the strip of grass beside the bus stop, her back wheel propped on its side and her tyre levers lined up on the pavement like silver spoons. The front tyre had gone flat on the ride to school, and Mr. Nikolaidis, waiting for the 42 with his newspaper under his arm, had said, "Well, there's your project for the morning," and then stayed to watch, which she suspected he regretted.

The trouble was the levers. She slid the first one under the tyre's edge, pushed down, and hooked it to a spoke like the video had shown. The second lever went in a hand-width away. She moved them around the rim, and the tyre's edge finally popped loose, letting her expose the tube underneath, pale and wrinkled as an empty balloon. Her friend Ciaran arrived at the run, took one look, and flopped onto the bench with dramatic despair. "We're going to be late, and I'm going to have to tell the office I was delayed by a bicycle surgery."

"You could help," Everly said. She ran her fingers along the inside of the tyre, hunting for whatever had caused the flat, because she'd read that the sharp thing usually stayed hidden there, waiting to strike twice. Her fingertip found it: a tiny sliver of glass, thin as a fingernail. She held it up to the light, and Ciaran, despite himself, leaned over to look. "It's like a shark tooth," he said. "A really tiny, useless shark."

She patched the tube, waited for the glue to set while two buses came and went, then tucked it back into the tyre and began wrestling the tyre back onto the rim with her thumbs. Mr. Nikolaidis folded his newspaper and offered to hold the wheel steady, which helped more than she expected. Then she attached the pump to the valve and started pumping. She pumped hard, arms aching, and nothing happened. The tube stayed as limp as before. She pumped again, harder, and the pump made a rude noise that had Ciaran snorting with laughter. "Your pump is broken," he declared. "It's unanimous. The pump has voted, and it votes no."

Everly stared at the valve. It didn't look like the one in the video, which had been fat and squat like a tiny mushroom. Hers was thin, with a small nut sitting on top of it. She gave the nut an experimental twist, and it turned, loosening. "It's a Presta valve," she said, mostly to herself, because she remembered the word now from the comments under the video, where someone had complained about exactly this. "This nut on top has to be unscrewed before any air can go in or out." She unscrewed it fully, clipped the pump on, and pushed. This time the pump moved with resistance, the tube fattened, and the tyre rose round and firm under her hands.

She spun the wheel, listening for any wobble, and it ran smooth and quiet. Mr. Nikolaidis checked his watch and said the next bus was theirs. Ciaran picked up the glass shard, wrapped it in a tissue, and presented it to Everly with a bow. "For your museum," he said. She pocketed it, wheeled her bike onto the bus, and called back over her shoulder, "Next time you get a flat, you're on your own."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The porch light went out first, then the kitchen window, then every glowing square on the whole street. Savannah was in the backyard checking the rain gauge she had mounted on the fence post, and she noticed the change the way you notice a sound stopping: not the darkness itself, but the absence of the light that had been there. The gauge held two centimetres of precipitation from the afternoon storm, and she had been about to record it in her weather notebook when the world behind her went black. She stood still for a moment, listening. Somewhere down the block a dog barked twice and stopped.

She found the back door by memory, one hand on the cool siding, and stepped into a kitchen she could no longer see. Her grandmother's voice came from the hallway, calm but hesitant, the way it sounded when she wasn't sure where the furniture was. "Savannah? Are you outside or in?"

"I'm in, Grandma. Stay where you are, I'm coming to you." Savannah moved slowly, arms out, until her fingers found the counter, then the drawer handle beside the sink. She knew this drawer. She had organized it herself last month, and she had allocated one half to batteries and the other half to flashlights, two big ones and a small one, after the fire-safety unit in Ms. Katz's class. Her hand slid past a roll of tape and closed around the rubber grip of the biggest light.

Her grandmother had already reached the pantry, though. When Savannah clicked the flashlight on, the beam caught her standing at the shelf with a box of candles in one hand and a matchbook in the other. "There we are," her grandmother said. "We'll have some light in a minute."

"Wait." Savannah crossed the room and set the second flashlight on the counter between them. "Ms. Katz drilled this into us. Safety agencies say to use flashlights, not candles, during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house." She picked up the candle box and set it back on its shelf, high up, out of the way. "I knocked a candle over at home once, before we ever had this unit. I know how fast it goes."

Her grandmother looked at the matchbook in her hand, then at the flashlight glowing steadily on the counter, and put the matches down beside the returned candles. "Well," she said, "I suppose that's why they let your teacher teach." She picked up the flashlight and swept the beam across the ceiling, across the window, and out toward the backyard, where the rain gauge caught the light for a second like a small glass lantern.

They carried the flashlights out to the porch steps and sat side by side, watching the dark street. Savannah wrote her precipitation number in the notebook by flashlight, printing carefully. Somewhere far off, a siren rose and faded, and the stars over the rooftops came out brighter than usual, filling in where the porch light used to be.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Nathaniel stood at the counter of the community kitchen with a raw chicken in front of him and no idea how to tell when it would be done. His mother had flu, his father was working late, and his little sister had announced she was hungry enough to eat a whole bird. That was why Nathaniel, Gage, and Charles-Antoine were all wearing aprons on a Tuesday evening, staring at Ms. Chen's big oven.

"You just cook it until it looks done," Gage said, sliding the tray toward the oven. "My dad does that all the time."

"That's guessing," Charles-Antoine said. He was the most hesitant cook among them, and he wanted tonight to go perfectly, because his grandmother was coming to taste whatever he helped make. "I don't want to guess with chicken."

Nathaniel turned the bird over, thinking. Guessing by color had to be the reason his uncle once served chicken that was pink near the bone, even though the outside was golden brown. The outside and the inside were two different things, and the outside always finished first. The hidden part, the thickest part, was the part that mattered. There had to be a way to check the inside directly instead of judging by the surface.

In the drawer below the spices he found a metal probe with a dial, a food thermometer, with a small card taped to its case. He read it twice. Poultry was safely cooked when its thickest part reached 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius. "This is it," he said. "We don't classify it as done by looking at it. We measure it."

He slid the probe into the thickest part of the thigh, careful not to touch bone, and watched the needle climb while the others crowded close. At 150 the skin looked completely done, golden and crisp, exactly like the pictures in cookbooks. Nathaniel kept waiting. At 160 Charles-Antoine said, "It looks done to me," but Nathaniel shook his head. At 165 the needle steadied, and he pulled the tray out.

They portioned the chicken onto plates, saved some for Nathaniel's family in a labeled container, and set aside the crispiest piece for Charles-Antoine's grandmother. Ms. Chen came by to collect the thermometer and found it washed and back in its drawer. "You checked the thickest part?" she asked.

"Seventy-four Celsius," Nathaniel said. "The card was right there in the case."

Charles-Antoine's grandmother arrived just as they carried the plates to the table, took one bite, and patted her grandson on the shoulder. "So," she said, "who is the chef among you three?"

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
The piano at Grandpa's house had a cracked bench and one key that stuck in humid weather, and Michael loved it anyway. Every Saturday he rode his bike over and practiced the piece Ms. Mansour had assigned, a short sonatina full of markings he was still decoding. Today he had a real problem: the recital was in two weeks, and Grandpa had said the piece sounded like one long drone.

"It's all the same speed," Grandpa said from his armchair. "The paper says otherwise, doesn't it?"

Michael scowled at the sheet. Near the top of the second line sat the word rit., and he knew that one; it meant slow down. He had been slowing down there for weeks. The trouble came after. Grandpa was right. Once Michael slowed, he stayed slow, dragging through the rest of the page like a tired hiker, and the lively ending collapsed.

After his ride home, he texted Monroe, who had been playing piano longer. "Do you ever get stuck slow after a rit?" Monroe wrote back a single clue: "Look for the tiny words right after." Michael dug out the music at school before band. Right after the slowing section, two small words sat above the staff: a tempo. He didn't recognize them. He copied them into his notebook and thought about them all through lunch, turning them over the way Yannick turned over beetles in science class. A tempo. Tempo meant speed. A meant... what?

At band practice, Ms. Mansour had them play a warm-up with a big slow-down in the middle, and then, exactly on cue, the whole group snapped back to the opening pace. Michael watched her finger touch the score, right where a tempo was printed. He grinned so wide that Yannick, next to him on trumpet, raised an eyebrow.

"That's it," Michael whispered. "A tempo. It means go back to the original speed after you slowed down."

"Or sped up," Yannick whispered back, pointing at a spot where the flutes had rushed.

Saturday, Michael integrated the discovery into his whole approach. He played the rit., let the music stretch like taffy, and then, at the words a tempo, he lifted back into the opening speed, steady as a heartbeat. Grandpa set down his newspaper. Michael played it three more times, and each time the ending came out brighter, the final chords ringing through the dilapidated old room like it had good news to share.

"Again," Grandpa said, folding the paper away entirely.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
Sara had ninety minutes until the judges reached her table, and her mystery liquids were still unlabeled. That was the whole point of her project, "Invisible Chemistry": visitors would dip litmus paper into six unmarked cups and use the pH scale to decide whether each solution was an acid or a base. The blue paper turning red meant acid. Red paper turning blue meant base. She had tested everything twice at home, except cup number five.

"Where's cup five from?" Dash asked, leaning over her table with his clipboard. He was manning the registration desk but kept wandering over.

"My grandma's bathroom. Soap dissolved in water," Sara said. "I tested the vinegar, the lemon juice, the baking soda water, everything else. Cup five I ran out of time for."

Ms. Vu stopped at the neighboring table, and Sara felt her stomach tighten. Ms. Vu was the toughest judge at the fair, the one who asked questions that could hinder even the best projects, questions nobody could wiggle out of. Last year she had disqualified a robot project because the student couldn't explain a single wire. There was nothing arbitrary about her rules, everyone said; she just caught whatever you hadn't bothered to learn.

The clock on the gym wall said 10:12. Sara tore off a strip of red litmus paper. Then she hesitated, because a thought had crept up on her: soap was for cleaning, and lemon juice was an acid, so maybe soapy water was an acid too, just a nicer-smelling one. The pattern felt right. Patterns could be wrong.

"Test it," Dash whispered.

She dipped the red strip into cup five. Slowly, while Sara held her breath and a mother with two little kids stopped to watch, the paper turned blue. Not a hint of pink. Blue, the opposite direction from the vinegar cup, which had turned blue paper red minutes ago. So soapy water sat on the other end of the scale entirely.

"It's a base," Sara said out loud, almost surprised at herself. Then, to the watching mother, "Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10."

"I didn't know that," the mother said.

"Neither did I, one hour ago."

At 10:24, Ms. Vu arrived. She dipped papers into every cup, asked Sara what would happen if she mixed the lemon cup and the soap cup, and listened while Sara reasoned it out. Then she picked up cup five and sniffed it.

"Interesting choice," Ms. Vu said. "My mother uses this exact soap."

Sara grinned. "So does mine."

Ms. Vu wrote something on her pad and moved on, and Dash slid a folded note across the table. Sara opened it. You labeled the cups wrong. Vinegar is in cup six. She looked up at the row of cups, at the little marks she'd scratched on the bottoms, and at the lemon juice sitting exactly where vinegar should have been.

"Fix it," Dash said. "Fast."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
Nathan had one job at the spring cultural festival: collect six signatures for Ms. Byrne's story wall, one from each booth, and each person had to write a sentence about where their family came from. Five booths down, his clipboard was almost full. The sixth booth sat at the end of the row, draped in red cloth, where an old woman was teaching kids to fold paper cranes while a girl about Nathan's age chatted with her in quick, bouncing syllables he didn't understand.

"Hi, I need one more signature," Nathan said, holding out the clipboard. "For the story wall."

The girl, who introduced herself as Hope, translated for the woman, who must have been her grandmother. The grandmother nodded, took the pen, and wrote something across the line in beautiful, crowded characters. Then she smiled and turned to help another kid with a crane.

"Great," Nathan said, and then stopped. "Wait. What does it say? Ms. Byrne wants us to know what each sentence means, for the display."

Hope's face went pink. "I don't know," she admitted. "I can talk to her fine, but reading is different. Nobody ever taught me the writing." She frowned at the line of ink like it was a locked door. "I ask her to say things out loud and I just answer."

Nathan turned this over. A language could live in your ears and your mouth but not in your eyes. He tested the idea out loud. "So you could tell me anything she says, but not anything she writes?"

"Exactly," Hope said. "It's a heritage language. That's what it's called when it's the language of your home and family, and it's different from what everyone else around here speaks."

Nathan glanced at the clock above the food stalls. The story wall closed in twenty minutes. He scanned the row of booths: a man selling a memoir about crossing an ocean, tables of bread and honey, a dancer winding up in a dragon costume so long and predatory that little kids backed away from its leaping head. The grandmother knew the words. Somebody here had to know the writing.

He tried the memoir booth first. The author looked at the clipboard, then read the sentence slowly, like he was tasting it. "It says, 'My home lives in my granddaughter's voice.'"

Hope stared at the paper, then at her grandmother, who was watching them both with her hands folded, waiting. She hadn't needed the translation at all.

"Okay," Hope said quietly, and took the pen. "Okay. I want to learn to read it. Starting today."

She wrote her name on the next line, and her grandmother laughed and pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward them both.

"Your turn, Hope," the old woman said, and tapped the first character with one crooked finger.
